rv.q: That nonstop naughtiness is what makes Martin McDonagh’s killer satire the best new play on Broadway by a green mile.

It’s a fabulous offering — a throwback, really, to the heyday of juicy, creepy London imports by McDonagh (“Pillowman”), Conor McPherson (“Shining City”), Mark Ravenhill and Jen Butterworth (“Jerusalem”).
And no one does dark impulses with as much comedic flare – yes, it’s sneaky, menacing and funny – as McDonagh at full tilt.
Happily (if such a word would apply to any of his work), this Broadway production is a deadly beauty, flawlessly cast and directed in the mordant style of an executioner’s song by Matthew Dunster.

Mr. McDonagh is incapable of writing a dull character or a flaccid line of dialogue, and “Hangmen” is peopled with a savory array of misfits and idlers propping up Harry’s bar, drawn in bold but never garish comic colors, unwittingly dispensing wit.
McDonagh’s cynicism feels closer to our own, or rather we to it.
Allen as Mooney hasn’t got the gravity, or the menace.
Beneath its slick coating, it's a slack exercise that in retrospect makes almost no sense at all.
“Hangmen” thoroughly wrings its premise dry, but anyone trying to find deeper meaning in McDonagh’s play will be left hanging.
Once you realize that McDonagh’s M.O. is crudely to undermine expectations, you expect the undermining, and boredom sets in.
“Hangmen” is this Broadway season’s best play.

“Hangmen” is a meticulously-plotted work containing eccentric characters and built upon elements of pub drama, physical farce, whodunit mystery, action thriller and legal drama – not to mention a noose and countless pints of cask ale.
Hangmen is the kind of play we don't really see anymore.
Luckily (if not unexpectedly), there’s a huge payoff in Act II, which is where McDonagh’s gifts for melding black comedy, tragedy and surprise come together with peerless skill.
Hilarious, searing, and poignant, the play presents a savage indictment of capital punishment without ever stooping to preach — a practice foreign to Mr. McDonagh.

"the cheerful brutality of [McDonagh's] work can sometimes betray a certain emptiness at the core; what are the stakes, when even a fatal miscarriage of justice is played for punchlines? Hangmen suffers from some of that dissonance, and its longer, talkier interludes serve more as amiable time fillers than story engine.

The first New York production of Hangmen had a creepier aura; this one—slickly directed by Matthew Dunster—leans more heavily into comedy, capitalizing on Threlfall’s purposely pompous puffed-chest, poker-faced delivery of the most wonderfully absurd lines.
Nonetheless, Hangman remains a wickedly perverse delight for theatergoers possessing the stomach and fortitude to go along for the ride.
The pair are worth the long wait and feature spectacular staging and tight-knit ensembles.

"As in all of [McDonagh's] plays, guilt and innocence are front and center as a theme and the miscarriage of justice, the ending of the death penalty, the uses and abuses of vengeance, and the psychological impact of violence on its perpetrators are the basis for the play.

Broadway hasn't had a good thriller in a long while, and Hangmen fits that bill quite nicely.
Martin McDonagh has been specializing in his own brand of bloodstained comedy for a quarter of a century now, so it's probably inevitable that the blood might get a little tired.
It takes a lot of work to pull things back together after a break of four years, and an ensemble work like this requires exquisite timing and consistency, elements that are, alas, in short supply.
But things have happened in the world since then, and I had a rush of reactions, none of which came close to amusement, when a character in “Hangmen” is being choked, and says “Can’t breathe.”
This unblendable mix of styles pretty much deflates and flattens the deliciously written denouement.
Macabre as this latter may sound, there’s no question Hangmen is a well-executed piece of capital entertainment.

cn.t: McDonagh's pitch-black comedy about England's last hangman delivers his signature dark humor and menace, though critics split on whether it reaches his best work or recycles familiar ideas with less impact.

sg.ra: 805-seat intimate Shubert house; center Orchestra D-F is the consensus best pick across Headout, SeatPlan, and TickPick. Rows A-D play well for plays/intimate-drama given Golden's small footprint. SeatPlan notes mezzanine overhang begins at Row L with 'minimal' effect, so orchestra rear rows remain viable.
Headout and TickPick both flag center G-L as the sweet spot for value — priced below front orchestra but still before the Row L overhang line. In an 805-seat house these rows feel close regardless.

Front Mezz rows A-C center are the #2 premium pick after center orchestra — elevation gives a clean overhead line on the small Golden stage. SeatPlan flags a safety bar that can distract Row A slightly, and legroom is noted as 'slightly cramped for taller patrons.'

SeatPlan calls rear mezz 'surprisingly good' because the 805-seat footprint keeps even back rows close. Rake is described as well-designed with good elevation over Front Mezz. Legroom is the main knock — 'cramped' with narrow pitch.
